prize_parts.citation: For a visionary, densely patterned Romanian prose and poetry in which memory, the body and dream are built into a metaphysical imaginative world of rare scale and formal ambition.

statement.case_for: My preference remains Mircea Cărtărescu, and I base it on the literary case, not on the fact that the opening rankings point the same way. On the common criteria: (1) Voice: the densely patterned, visionary prose of Blinding and Solenoid is recognizable as no one else's. (2) Formal and linguistic achievement: the work builds long architectonic structures that keep their density, and the poetry is a base for the prose rather than a separate sideline. (3) Imaginative and intellectual depth: memory, the body and metaphysical speculation form one project, not a set of effects. (4) Sustained quality: the work has a long cumulative arc in which later books extend earlier ones, so the reputation does not rest on a single title. A citation can name this project in a single sentence. Authorship is unambiguous and the scope covers poetry and fiction without needing to stretch the category of literature in Nobel's will. This is also a case I can argue in terms of language and form, not mainly in terms of theme or symbolism.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the case depends on prose whose effect is tied to Romanian sentence rhythm and density, and I can judge it only through public knowledge and translations that may flatter or flatten it. The sprawling architecture may also be uneven across volumes, and what sustains the metaphysical density across the whole corpus, rather than in the best-known novels, is not settled. Coverage of the poetry and early work is thinner than coverage of the major novels, so a citation spanning poetry and prose rests on less secure evidence for the poetic strand. Last, my own scholarly interests (modern poetry, the fragment, nihilism and mysticism) are context only, not evidence of preference, but they are a reason to test whether I am overvaluing a metaphysical, inward project, and I want the committee to press that point.

responses.point: Mattson ranks Can Xue second for an uncompromising, original fictional method in which dreamlike worlds destabilize psychology, space and causality. She sees the radicalism as sustained rather than occasional, while noting that translation is a major filter.
responses.response: I ranked Can Xue last of my eight, and Mattson's argument is a fair challenge to that. Formal radicalism held for decades is a real merit under the criteria of voice and sustained quality, and I should not treat consistency as a defect in itself. My remaining doubt is narrower than Mattson's: I cannot tell from translation whether the method deepens across the corpus or repeats one mode, and whether the philosophical depth is in the prose or partly supplied by interpretation. Mattson shares that uncertainty about translation. I would therefore want evidence of development within the work, for example how the later novels differ in kind from the early stories, before moving her above Cărtărescu, whose arc seems to me easier to trace. I accept that the case is stronger than my opening ranking implied.

responses.point: Carlberg puts Adonis second on formal and linguistic achievement, as a poet who reshaped modern Arabic poetry through myth, fragmentation and critical dialogue with the classical tradition. She flags that translation loses much of this and that his essays and public positions must not replace literary merit.
responses.response: I agree with Carlberg's framing and have Adonis second myself. I also agree on the central difficulty: the claim is mainly about prosody and diction, which is exactly what translation loses, so the committee leans on reputation and secondary accounts more than I would like. I would keep the citation on the poetry and treat the essays as context, and I would not let his public statements count either way. My difference with Carlberg is one of confidence, not of direction. For Cărtărescu the translated prose still conveys architecture and scale, whereas the case for Adonis depends more on features I cannot test. That is why I hold him as the principal alternative and not as my first choice. Expert reports on Arabic poetry would carry real weight here.

responses.point: Palm places Lídia Jorge second, for a sustained novelistic oeuvre on colonial war, memory and gender, with ironic, layered narration and moral and historical intelligence beyond subject matter. She also describes Cărtărescu's major works as an integrated body, not isolated peaks.
responses.response: I accept Palm's point about integration. It matches what I find strongest in Cărtărescu, and it is the answer to the worry that his reputation rests on one or two titles. On Jorge, I did not rank her, so I owe a clear reason. It is not that the work is minor: the handling of fragmented testimony and the historical conscience are real strengths. My doubt is whether her voice is singular enough, in what I can judge through translation, to separate her from other serious historical novelists in the same tradition. Sward raises a similar question about distinctiveness. If Palm can name the passages or devices where the narration is unlike anything else, such as the structure of testimony in The Murmuring Coast, I would reconsider. As it stands I do not think the case is yet made on voice.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg values Cărtărescu's scale and architectonic density and notes the poetry at the base of the oeuvre, and he also ranks Pierre Michon fourth for compressed, highly worked French prose, where quality rests on style rather than volume.
responses.response: I agree that the poetry is the base of Cărtărescu's prose and that this supports linguistic command beyond the novels, though I would want the poetry examined directly rather than inferred. On Michon, I see a real linguistic achievement, and I do not think brevity disqualifies him: a small, exact body of work can meet the standard of sustained quality. My hesitation is that the case rests almost entirely on sentence-level style, which is the feature English translation conveys least, and the small corpus gives less to judge for range and development. I did not place him in my eight, but Sem-Sandberg's emphasis on compression over volume is a fair criterion that I would not dismiss on size alone.

uncertainties: Translation: the Cărtărescu case depends on the density and rhythm of Romanian prose, and how far translations convey it is unresolved. Poetry-based alternatives (Adonis, Carson) depend even more on features that translation loses.
Corpus coverage: the poetry and early work of Cărtărescu are less visible in translation than the major novels, so the poetic strand of the citation is less secure.
Whether the metaphysical density is sustained across the whole corpus or concentrated in the best-known novels cannot be settled from public knowledge alone.
For Can Xue, it is unresolved whether the method develops across decades or repeats, and how much of the translated corpus is representative.
I rely on public knowledge and the supplied descriptions, and have not independently verified texts or read the full corpus in any language.
Whether the committee's anonymous regional expert reports bear on candidates writing in Arabic, Chinese or Japanese is not something I can establish from the supplied evidence.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. The listed connections (Horace Engdahl, Daniel Birnbaum, the Kris circle, and the scholarly work on Ekelöf, Celan, exile literature and the fragment) show no link to Cărtărescu or to the other shortlisted writers. My scholarly interests are context, not evidence of preference.
